utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody. The next witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Please wait a moment so that the screens could be opened. Good afternoon, sir, again. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card to tell the truth, which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You know that there are still protective measures in place for you, and Ms. Chittenden has some questions for you. Ms. Chittenden.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. We met on Sunday. My name is Caitlin Chittenden, and I'll be asking you some questions today on behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Please, could we have Exhibit P727 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Witness, you'll see something coming up on the screen in front of you now. Please, could you read it to yourself and confirm that your name is written next to "PW-076."

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: And it should not be broadcast, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to tender this as an exhibit under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall providing a statement via the telephone to the Office of the Prosecutor on 30 June 2010?

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Have you had the opportunity to review that draft witness statement before coming here today?

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Was your statement truthful and accurate?

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: If you were asked the same questions again in court today, would you answer in the same way?

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I would like to offer into evidence the witness's draft statement to the Office of the Prosecutor on 30 June 2010 as an exhibit under seal. It is Exhibit P725.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Witness, did you finalise that draft witness statement when you met with the Office of the Prosecutor in person on 22 August 2010?

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Did you have that statement read back to you in your own language?

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Is that witness statement truthful and accurate?

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Did you sign that statement?

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: If you were asked the same questions again in court today, would you answer in the same way?

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Please, could we have Exhibit P726 in e-court, in English and B/C/S, and this should not be broadcast, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Witness, if you take a look at the screen in front of you. Please take a look at both the English and the B/C/S versions of the document, which are on the screen. On the English version, on the right, at the bottom of the page, can you let me know if that's your signature?

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Witness, is this the statement that you finalised and signed at the offices of the Prosecutor when we met on Sunday, 22 August 2010?

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I would also like to admit into evidence this signed version of the witness's statement, dated 22 August 2010. This is the signed version of the 30 June draft witness statement which was provisionally admitted pursuant to your oral ruling yesterday. For your information, the signed statement is the same as the draft, except that it also includes the witness's review and confirmation of the six intercepts and a few short comments he made in relation to that and also in relation to his role as an intercept operator. The statement, the signed version, has disclosed to the accused in English and in B/C/S on Sunday afternoon. However -- sorry, and it was also included on our proposed exhibit list. However, if Your Honours do not wish for the signed statement to be admitted at this time, I can lead the witness on the additional information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In this case, because it appears to be -- to have the same content as the previously admitted statement, we would like to see the statement and if it contains a reference to the intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Of course, yes. I have -- we can look at the version on the screen. If you like, I have a hard copy, but I've put some highlight on it. But I might have a clean copy here. Thank you. If I could ask for the Court Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The statement is in e-court?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: That's correct, yeah, and it's Exhibit P726. The Court Usher has just handed you a draft and the final version, just so you can have a look at both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm a little bit -- I don't understand why we receive now the hard copies of both the 22nd of August statement and the 30th of June statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: That's correct, just in case you wanted to look at both, but the one I'm proposing is the 22 August final statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If it's in e-court, then that's fine, and you should deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. Thank you, Your Honours. Your Honours, I would now like to read a short summary of the witness's draft and final statement, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Witness, after I've read out the summary, I'll have a few further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we may move into private session for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: At the southern site, the witness's detachment worked in shifts of six hours, followed by a break of twelve hours when they were off duty. The witness performed the duties of an intercept operator. He followed the established practice at the southern site for intercepting, recording, and transcribing VRS communications into note-books. If the participants in an intercepted conversation were unknown, they would be marked as X and Y. If the witness was unable to hear any part of a conversation clearly, he would consult his colleagues and commander, and together they would listen to the conversation to try to determine what was being said. If they were unable to determine what was said, the witness would put several dots or write "Unintelligible." Once the conversation was transcribed, it would be forwarded to the typist, who would type, date, and transmit reports of conversations to the command. The witness did not type up or transmit any recorded conversations, and it was not the witness's duty, as an intercept operator, to date every intercept he recorded in the note-books. Your Honours, that concludes my summary. I now have a few questions to ask the witness, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Witness, I would like to show you a booklet of six intercepts that we have compiled.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: If I can just ask for the assistance of the Court Usher to pass it to the witness. For the record, these are Exhibits P728A and B, through 733A and B.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Witness, can you take a moment to look through each of the six tabs in this booklet, and let me know whether you recognise your handwriting on the handwritten versions of the six intercepts.

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Take your time and look through all six of them, just to make sure.

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Witness, were you the operator who recorded and transcribed these six intercepted conversations?

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Did you review these six intercepts before you testified today?

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Did you also review the original note-books containing these six intercepts?

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Do the copies of those six intercepts conform to the original note-books that you reviewed?

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Did you also review the print-out versions of these intercepts?

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: And do the printed versions reflect the same conversations as the handwritten versions of the intercepts?

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I would like to admit into evidence the handwritten and print-out versions of these six intercepts. And for the record, these are P728 through P733.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: They will be received.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: I just now have a few brief questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Witness, can you briefly describe for the Trial Chamber what your duties were as an intercept operator at the southern site?

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: As I did my job honestly, with earphones on my head, I was supposed to transcribe the conversations and hand them over. That was my job.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Where did you transcribe these conversations?

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: I used the note-books.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: And you mentioned handing them over. Who did you hand them over to?

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: To whoever was in charge and to whoever was duty-bound to forward those note-books to an operator.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Witness, do you know -- you mentioned handing them over to whoever was in charge or who was duty-bound to forward them. Do you know what this person did with the information contained in the note-books once you had passed it over to them?

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Witness, who put the date on the intercepted conversations?

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: The operator who typed them up.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Thank you. And is that the same operator you were just referring to before?

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: Yes, yes, a person whose job that was.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: And just to clarify for the transcript, he was referring to operator on page 8, lines 25, and page 9, lines 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Witness, what did you do if you couldn't hear any part of a conversation?

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: The commander would then listen to the tape again, together with two other members of our team.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: What would happen if no one could determine what was being said in the conversation?

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: It either remained unclear and noted as such or that portion of the conversation was replaced by little dots.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: As I have indicated earlier, we would like to see the second statement of August 2010 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Okay. If we could have P726 in e-court, please. And this should not be broadcast. It's -- would you like to turn through the pages or what's the -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The content of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Pardon me? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The content of the statement is of interest because we saw only the previous one, and we have heard that you didn't intend to tender this document into evidence. Therefore, I would like to see the difference of --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Of course. So let's go to page 2, please, in e-court. And I can specifically tell you what's different. In the English version, you can see paragraph 7, and the new line -- sorry, there's two new sentences at the end: "I did not analyse any conversations." And: "My duty was only to listen to, record, and transcribe intercepted conversations into note-books." That's new. Paragraph 9, after the typist would put a date. That is new, the remainder of that paragraph. And if we can go to the third page, the main change or the main update of this statement is, as I referred to, the six intercepts that were shown to the witness, and that is from paragraphs 12, 13, 14, 15, and for the rest of the statement. So you can see the top, in paragraph 12, a list of the handwritten versions of the intercepts, with the exhibit numbers on the left, and then paragraph 15, the printed versions, with the exhibit numbers on the left. And for the record, those are the same exhibits I showed the witness in the booklet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I ask you, the witness, if you recall to have signed this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This document will be received as P726, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I suppose this concludes your examination-in-chief. Thank you very much. Now, Mr. Tolimir, it's your turn. If you have cross-examination, please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to welcome everybody present. May God's peace reign in this house, and may God's will be done in these proceedings and not necessarily mine. I would like to welcome the witness and I wish him a pleasant stay in our midst. Can the Court please produce the witness's statement, P726. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please tell us how come he did not sign the statement in his own mother tongue? Is it possible that he understands English so much better? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: It was never provided to me. I was not provided with a statement in my own language.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And now can you please tell us how come your statement was provided over the phone, and also who was it who approached you to ask for your statement? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: Could you please repeat?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please tell us or tell the Trial Chamber how come you provided the statement over the phone on the 10th [as interpreted] of June, 2010, and who was it who approached you to ask you for your statement and who prepared you for the statement?

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: People from the Tribunal. I don't have a clue, really. A lady called Marija, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you tell the Trial Chamber whether before that you had a discussion about that with somebody from the BiH Army, and did you ask their permission to testify before the Court?

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: When you served in the JNA, was it in units for electronic surveillance and anti-electronic intelligence, as you stated in your statement?

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: Yes, one part of my service entailed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And did you also work in the Electronic Interception Service?

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the Court please produce the second page of this statement, because my next few questions will concern that part of his statement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, in paragraph 4, line 2, you say that you joined the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and that you were a member of the 121st Mountain Brigade. Could you please tell us whether, as a member of that unit, you also belonged to a communications unit?

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 4, line 3, you say that before joining the team on the southern site, you had come directly from that unit. Had you undergone any training or education to work on radio intercept equipment?

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: For the record, it's paragraph 5 and not paragraph 4, I think. But paragraph 4 has only two lines.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, for the correction. You are absolutely right, it was paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In paragraph 6, you say about working in shifts -- you speak about working in shifts. Could you please tell us whether you were able to perform all of your duties during one shift if there were only two of you in one shift? Could you perform all the duties and all your tasks?

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: If the workload was more substantial, we were helped by other team members.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. In paragraph 7, you described the procedure that you were involved in. Could you please describe for the Trial Chamber what jobs did you do as a radio intercept operator?

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: It was very simple. There was a frequency, there were headphones, there was a UHER for recording, and later on we copied everything, and that was all. That's the long and the short of my job. And then before we gave our notes to somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not clear. When you say "copy," can you explain for the Trial Chamber what you copied and where from?

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: Everything was recorded on UHER, on cassettes, and from cassettes we copied what we heard into note-books and forwarded them to somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you use papers first and then copied those notes into note-books or did you go directly from what you heard?

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: We went directly with what we heard. We noted it in the note-books. And then if we didn't understand that, we had to do it all over again, we had to listen to the tapes again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us whether you have ever seen, while you were in the unit, in A4 format, whether you have ever seen a typed-up transcript of these intercepts that were being recorded, such as the ones that were shown to us by Ms. Chittenden? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us, please, when was it that you saw typed-up transcripts for the first time, typed on A4 sheets of paper?

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: Here in the courtroom. Or, actually, on Saturday during -- or Sunday/Monday, during the proofing session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, in paragraph 8, you talk about how these intercepts were made during the times when there was good -- when you could hear them clearly or not. And then you say that then you would decide to meet, a number of you, to discuss them. Now, could you please tell us what it was -- or on the basis of what was it that you decided what was being said if you were unable to hear it properly?

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: Well, we would usually leave that it's indiscernible or we would put three dots.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please take a look at paragraph 8, line 4. You say: "We would listen to the transcript together in order to determine what was said." So tell us, did you actually determine what was said or did you just put "unintelligible"?

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: Well, in 80 per cent of the cases, we would just put "unintelligible" or put three dots.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I remind both speakers to pause between question and answer. It is very difficult for the interpreters and the record to catch everything what was said. Please pause between question and answer. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, because we speak in the same language, please, let's make a brief pause after our questions or answers. So you used the word "determine" what was being said. On the basis of what, in those 20 per cent of the cases, did you determine what was being said?

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: Well, if we could determine what was being said and if all three of us would have the same opinion that it was that particular word, then we would determine that that's what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Witness. Would you now tell us, please, whether you entered or corrected errors in the logs, if later on you were able to verify or correct them, or would you just leave it as it was? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: Well, we would add "unclear" to that portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. For instance, if you were to write down a word, and then you realised that that was not the word used during the conversation, the intercepted conversation, would you cross it out or would you just leave "unclear" or "unintelligible" in brackets? So if later on you realised that it was not really unclear or unintelligible, but that actually the intercept operator had made a mistake in hearing it, what would you do?

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: Well, yes --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat? Could the witness repeat the answer? He was not very clear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the intercept operator and two other members would later on look at the -- listen to the intercept and look at the transcript. They would put the word "unclear" if something was unclear.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. But please listen carefully. Did it ever occur that you would write one word down, in one sense of the word that is used, and then later on it turns out that a speaker had said something else and this was confirmed by the other two persons who were listening to the intercept with you? What would you have done in such cases? Would you correct that word and put in the new word or would you just add this comment that it was not very intelligible and poor reception?

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: Poor reception and unintelligible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In these log-books that were shown to you by Ms. Caitlin, were there any instances where you had written this down, where you had put this note down, "unintelligible" or "unclear" or were there some instances where some words were crossed out?

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: Well, the log-books contained the note or remark "unclear" or three dots.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You are very much overlapping, and it's very clear and the interpreter has to ask for repetitions. So please bear in mind you need to pause, because you start answering or questioning. Carry on, please, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, the intercepts that you are testifying about here before this Court, do they contain any corrections, or any crossed-out words, or any words that would have the letter Y next to them? Because you told us that you have been able to review all these transcripts that you received on Sunday from Ms. Chittenden. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: Well, I do believe that there was one error.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You've said, and you say in paragraph 9, line 3, that the typist would put the date on or above the intercepted conversation that he would type over from the log-book. So did I understand this correctly? Is this true, that the typist actually was the one who established -- determined what the date was?

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: Well, no, he was not the one to determine it. He had to just copy down what was written.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please take a look at paragraph 9, line 3, and read it out. Thank you. Here we see it, it's on the first page. We have the end of the sentence. It starts there, and then it goes on to the next page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see page 3, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So this typist would put a date, those last three words we had on the previous page, and then if you look at the first line on this page, it says: "The intercepted conversations before transmitting them to the command." So my question is this: Why was the typist the one who had to date these intercepts? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: Well, probably he was ordered to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the typist also have access to the tapes that you made - thank you - the recordings?

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: The platoon commander and the typist. To the platoon commander and to the typist.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, I apologise, but for the transcript, could you please repeat your answer. Did the typist also receive the tapes that you made during your intercepts?

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: Yes, to the typist and to the platoon commander. These were sent to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the typist review or listen again to the intercepts and then make any corrections that you had possibly made while you transcribed them? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: The typist was in another room, and I can't really say what he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please take a look at paragraph 10. It will refresh your memory, hopefully, and I will just remind you. You said that you recall one of these intercepted conversations between the president of the republic, Radovan Karadzic, and a person that was on the other end of the line. And my question is this: Do you recall any conversations that I had with another person that you were able to intercept and record? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: Well, 15 years down the road, 15 years later, it's hard to recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you had occasion two days ago to review these intercepts. Were you able to find among them any intercepted conversations that I had with anyone else, and do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: Well, the ones with the markings "X/Y" and the one where it's indicated that it's Zlatar and Palma, I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, thank you. But if you put X and Y for some speaker, is that something that can be assigned to a person who is being tried by the person transcribing, or do you at least know what radio network was used?

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: Well, that was not my job.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell us whether on Sunday, three days ago, you were shown by the Prosecutor any intercepts that you allegedly made of my conversations with people that I had conversations with. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: I looked and reviewed these transcripts. I only looked at them in the paper version.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. After you have reviewed the transcripts, and based on the paper trail, as you said, when you determined what the contents of those transcripts were, were you able to locate any transcripts where there were any conversations between me and some interlocutor? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: Well, I just told you a few moments ago that after 15 years, I can't really recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have the tapes of these intercepts that you are testifying about before this Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: No, I don't have them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Are these tapes kept within your unit or here in this Tribunal so that we can determine what these intercepts were and who the persons speaking were?

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: Well, I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us -- looking at the files that were provided to you by the Prosecutor, can you identify any words spoken by me in those transcripts that you are presenting to this Court as being the ones made by you?

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: Well, right now, no, I couldn't do it. Had I been asked to do this in 1999 or 2000, maybe I would have been able to recall, but 15 years later --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. But can you tell us, looking at the papers that you have before you, can you identify a single word spoken by me? Thank you. So I'm not asking you about 15 years ago. I'm asking you about a few days ago, since Sunday, because Ms. Chittenden asked you a few moments ago whether you were able to review the transcripts of the intercepts that you are testifying about and you said that you were given that opportunity.

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: Well, I reviewed these transcripts, but there are here also speakers denoted as X, Y, Zlatar, and Palma.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Can you tell us, please, why, in paragraphs 14 and 15 -- please take a look at them, they're before you. Why is it noted there, where we have these six intercepts under paragraph 15, that by error you typed the frequency number as one number and that this was corrected here at the Tribunal? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: Well, no, this correction was made in the command, as far as I could see from these papers, looking at the typewritten copies.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Chittenden.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Thank you. I would just like to clarify for the record that that's paragraph 19 that we're talking about from the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could we have that on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Ms. Chittenden.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: That is, indeed, in paragraph 19, where you mention that you wrote down, mistakenly, "Frequency 987," whereas the correct frequency was 897, as indicated and typed up in the intercept transcript. My question is this: A moment ago, when we discussed these matters, you said that you saw these typed-up versions for the first time here at the Tribunal. And I asked you then who had made that correction and on the basis of what, and you said that it was corrected at the corps command. Now, what was the basis for the corps command to correct this error? On the basis of what did they do this?

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it standard practice that the person to whom a telegraph is sent should enter any corrections in that text and correct the words noted by the intercept operator?

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Maybe my question wasn't clear enough, so let me rephrase it. Should the original contain only what was noted in your log-book, without the corrections being made, but rather with an additional remark being added that this should be corrected to reflect so-and-so? So wouldn't that be something to -- the right thing to do?

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, during your training, were you told what you were to do if you were to notice that there was an error subsequently, in other words, after had you already transcribed the intercept? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: I can't really recall as I sit here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please tell me, what kind of training did you undergo, excluding the period while you served in the JNA? So what all different types of training and where did you undergo?

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: Well, in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us, who was your instructor and what were you taught there?

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: Communications officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If the Trial Chamber were to give you some time now to leaf through the transcripts that you have before you, would you be able to point out any words that were spoken by me? And if you were to be given a tape, would you be able to recognise my voice? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: Well, 15 years is a long time, and I am not what I used to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. But if my voice were to be recorded, taped, now, would you recognise it? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: Well, the equipment is a bit different nowadays.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, thank you. But would you agree with me that each person has a very specific voice and that it's the -- the timbre of the voice is recognisable as much as a finger-print?

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: Well, I -- I'm not -- I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness, for your honest answers. Thank you for coming here, and I wish you all the best in your future life. And I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I would like to thank everyone who has helped me during this questioning, and I apologise to the interpreters and to the court reporter for speaking too fast at times. Your Honours, that's all I have to say. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tolimir. Ms. Chittenden, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: No, I don't, Mr. President. I just had one clarification on page 12, line 7. I think it was an inadvertent reference to the 10th of June instead of the 30th of June for the date of the statement. But no re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'd like to ask the witness: Do you recall the date when you had this telephone conversation with a member of the Prosecution? Was it the 30th of June or the 10th of June ?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the whole answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please repeat your whole answer, because your voice was very -- was not to be heard.

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: When was the first interview with me, me personally?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, on the phone.

utterances.speaker: PW-076
utterances.text: I can't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Mr. President, sorry. My clarification was actually in a question put to the witness, rather than the witness's answer. That's what I -- sorry. It said "10th of June" in the question. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. That clarifies the situation. Judge Mindua has a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do have a question, a short question. I think we could go into closed session, because I would like to ask the witness about his view on the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You will be pleased to know that you are now free to leave the Tribunal to return to your normal activities. The Chamber would like to thank you for your attendance here and for your patience to wait for your testimony. Thank you, again, and all the best wishes for your future. The Court Officer will assist you while leaving the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Chittenden and your colleagues, would that be, perhaps today, a convenient time for the first break in order to arrange everything for the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Then we should do that. We adjourn now, have our first break now, and resume 10 minutes before 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. May I remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth still applies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I suppose that Mr. Thayer has some additional questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I do, and thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon to you and to Your Honours. Good afternoon to the Defence. Good afternoon, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, before we continue, the Prosecution would tender Exhibit 1D00247. It is the communication from the ABiH General Staff, General Hadzihasanovic, of the 13 July [Realtime transcript read in error "30th of July"] at 1050 hours. It's a Defence exhibit in this case, as it was in the last case. We used it yesterday with the witness, and there's an English translation available in e-court. I'm not sure if its up-loaded yet. Some of the Defence exhibits were up-loaded as of this afternoon, but not all of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm trying to find it in your exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: It was not on our exhibit list, as I stated yesterday. It wasn't one of the documents I'd intended to use with the witness, but it came up spontaneously, as it were, during the examination. But as I said, it is a Defence exhibit in this case, so we would tender it at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The exhibit we have on the screen now?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You said -- but then, in that case, there must be a mistake on the transcript. Not the 30th of July, but the 13th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes. I may have misspoken. It is the 13th of July, not the 30th of July, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P734.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please go ahead, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We left off yesterday, Witness, with the meeting at the Boksanica check-point ending and you returning. Can you pick up from there, please?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the meeting at the check-point number 2, manned by UNPROFOR, Mujo Omanovic and I returned to Zepa. We travelled by UNPROFOR -- by an UNPROFOR vehicle. As we arrived in Zepa, we briefed other members of the War Presidency about the conditions or the ultimatum given to us at the meeting with General Tolimir. A meeting was held involving all War Presidency members. I believe that the meeting was quite long. It lasted a couple of hours. And at that meeting, we discussed the proposal we had heard, and the general feeling or the general conclusion as a result of that meeting was that we wouldn't accept the proposal and that we would not agree to all of the population being evacuated from the Zepa enclave, including the able-bodied men of Zepa. According to the agreement we had reached at check-point 2 with General Tolimir, we were supposed to convey our final decision to the main commander of UNPROFOR in Zepa, Colonel Dudnjik, and that's what we did. Let me briefly go back to the reasons why such decision had been made. The main reason for such a decision was our fear for the lives of able-bodied men or men between the ages of 18 and 55 or 60. That was the main reason, that fear was the main reason. And the decision was that we would not accept that proposal. After we informed General Dudnjik -- and to be honest, I don't remember -- rather, I apologise, not General Dudnjik, but Colonel Dudnjik, and I don't remember whether we conveyed the information in a written form or just orally. Pursuant to our previous agreement, Colonel Dudnjik was supposed to go back to check-point 2 and to convey our decision, or, rather, the decision of the War Presidency, to the Serb side. Speaking from memory, I can tell you that when Colonel Dudnjik left, and probably after he had conveyed our decision to the Serbian side, shelling started soon thereafter, the shelling of Zepa, or, rather, that was the beginning of a military operation against Zepa. Should I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just a couple of brief follow-ups, sir. Before the shelling began, did you or any of the members of the War Presidency have any contact with Colonel Dudnjik after he had conveyed the decision or the position of the Muslim authorities to the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that when it comes to our decision being conveyed to Dudnjik, I believe that Colonel Palic was in charge of that, and if I remember correctly, I believe that Colonel Palic told us that Dudnjik had been quite apprehensive about our decision. During that period, I did not have any contacts with Colonel Dudnjik after he returned to Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did Colonel Palic give you any sense of why Colonel Dudnjik was so apprehensive about your decision, sir?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember much of the detail of that. Most probably, Dudnjik believed, which later on proved to be correct, that Zepa didn't stand a chance and that it could not defend itself. He was of the opinion that we should have accepted the offer that had been made to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Please tell the Trial Chamber what was struck by the shelling that followed. What were the targets?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I can't remember everything. I believe that the main targets were the center of Zepa and the surrounding villages, but, really, I can't provide you with any more details. I'm sure that the center of Zepa was targeted. I'm positive of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Were civilian homes or buildings targeted, sir?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. As the situation developed and as attacks ensued, civilian homes and buildings were often targeted.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Was there armed resistance by the ABiH fighters in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The War Presidency held a meeting. After that, Avdo went to organise the resistance. I believe that on that same evening, a defence line was set up on the southern side facing Boksanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just generally speaking, sir, can you give the Trial Chamber an idea of what kind of a fight the ABiH forces in Zepa were able to put up, and for how long, and with what means?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I said yesterday during my testimony, based on the information that I had at the time, I would say that 600 men had weapons, mostly light infantry weapons, mostly AK-47, the famous Kalashnikov rifles. As far as I can remember, there was some anti-armour weaponry. I believe that those were rocket-launchers known as Red Arrow, if my memory serves me correctly. That's what had been air-dropped by helicopters. There were not that many of those weapons. I believe that Zepa had four pieces altogether. Again, speaking from memory, we didn't have any mortars, we didn't have any mortar shells in any case. Again, according to what I knew at the time, that was the armament that the BiH Army had at its disposal at the time in Zepa. The VRS attacks continued. As far as I can remember, in addition to the axis along the southern side in the direction of Rogatica, serious attacks came from the direction of the village of Godjenje. I would say that's the south-western side of the enclave. Lines were set up, and they were maintained. I don't know whether any of the lines were moved at places near the village of Godjenje or the line on the south-western side. It is possible that the VRS did make certain advances, but that was still not the key development leading to the fall of Zepa. I would like to go back and say that the ammunition for the light infantry weapons existed in very limited quantities, of course, and that was actually what was the main limitation, in view of the time of defence. The attacks continued. The lines -- the defence lines were not moved, as far as I can remember, up to the 19th of July, 1995. On the 19th of July, VRS attacks stopped. There was a lull. What ensued was a new invitation via UNPROFOR for a new round of talks at check-point 2 in Boksanica. I would like to point out one more thing at this time. At that time, we had very frequent contacts with our military and political leaderships in Sarajevo. We never received a clear answer as to what could be done in order to save Zepa. Thus, we realised that the matter was in our hands and that we were left to our own means. There was no other way, there was no other possibility. We couldn't expect help from anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, before we move into the events of the 19th of July, Witness, and again recognising that you're not a military man, but you clearly have a very good memory for these events, as you were there during the time and were very much involved as a part of the civilian authority, can you give the Trial Chamber an idea, please, of whether the terrain of Zepa affected the ABiH's ability to resist the attack up until the 19th, for example?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, the terrain and the geographical location of Zepa were two key factors which determined, in my view, the length of resistance against the VRS. And the VRS was much better armed. They had at their disposal all sorts of means and equipment. And that's what I already said at the very outset. Zepa has very well-delineated natural borders and a natural configuration which is conducive to an efficient defence, even with very little means available. And I'm talking about defence from military attacks. That means that all of the entrances into Zepa are naturally defined entrances in two or three points, and those points could be easily controlled. Tanks could not enter Zepa easily. Zepa is not in a low-lying land which would have been conducive to an easy advance of tanks, and that is the main reason, in my view, why Zepa was able to defend itself for such a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, did you learn at some point during the attack that Muslim fighters had over-run or, for lack of a better word, robbed weapons and equipment, ammunition, from some of the Ukrainian check-points?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that on the 13th -- or, rather, I can say no to your question, because I didn't know that. I'm not claiming that things like that didn't happen, but while those things were happening, I didn't know anything about them. But I know that Avdo Palic had gotten in touch with the Ukrainian Battalion, asking them to hand over the weapons that had been surrendered during the process of demilitarisation. I really don't know whether that happened, whether that materialised or not; if it did, who was in charge. Whatever I told you at this point, I would only be speculating, but I know that there was an idea of the kind. And as to whether the Ukrainian soldiers were robbed of their own weapons, whether any such thing happened, whether any of the check-points were over-run by BiH soldiers, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. You brought us up to the 19th of July. You said that you received, through UNPROFOR, another, to use your word, invitation. Who or what party, again, sir, originated or initiated this invitation to the Zepa authorities?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, I believe that Avdo received that invitation, in other words, Colonel Palic from the Ukrainian Battalion, and that the invitation was sent from check-point 2 by General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So from Mladic through Dudnjik or some Ukrainian to Palic, ultimately to you; is that how it went?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's how it went, that's correct. But I forgot to mention that on the 13th, after he left, Colonel Dudnjik did not return to the mission command in down-town Zepa, the UNPROFOR command. He remained at check-point 2. And as far as I can recall, and I can't remember the name of the person, but the main commander in Zepa of the Zepa mission was a younger officer, I believe a lieutenant, and it was via him that that invitation arrived. I believe that Palic and I -- Colonel Palic and I went to the UNPROFOR headquarters in Zepa, where, with the help of the radio, we talked with General Mladic, who was at check-point 2 at the time. After that radio communication, and we had already agreed earlier to go to check-point 3 one more time, and when discussing the request of General Mladic, we agreed that our representatives would go on that same day, in the afternoon, to check-point 2 at Boksanica. After some additional consultation at the War Presidency -- in fact, we didn't even have a meeting. The decision had been made immediately. It was decided, in other words, that I should go to check-point 2, the UNPROFOR check-point 2 at Boksanica, to meet with General Mladic, and that was for continuity purposes, because after July 12th and the events of July 12th, I was actually put in charge of contacts with the UNPROFOR and the Serb side, as well as Mr. Benjamin Kulovac. This was in late afternoon, I believe, perhaps around 3.00 p.m. or so. I can't really recall. We set off in an UNPROFOR vehicle to check-point 2. When we arrived at Boksanica, we were met by General Mladic. And if I'm not mistaken, I believe General Tolimir was there too. On the Serb side, and I'm not absolutely certain about this, but I think that Colonel Rajko Kusic was there too, and Colonel Dudnjik was there as an UNPROFOR representative. We sat around the table, which was outside, and General Mladic insisted that the evacuation of the population should start immediately. He dictated the demands, and as far as I can recall, they were as follows: First, the wounded would be evacuated, followed by women, children. And as for able-bodied men, they were to surrender their weapons to UNPROFOR. And then I can't recall exactly the phrasing of what followed, that they should be registered by the Red Cross or something to that effect, and, if I'm not mistaken, that there should then ensue an exchange on the principle of "all for all." Mr. Benjamin Kulovac and I -- and I apologise, but I would like to go back to the meeting and just say a few more things about the meeting there. The only person who spoke at the meeting was General Mladic. I jotted down his words, the words that Mladic dictated. And Benjamin Kulovac and I then went back to Zepa in the UNPROFOR vehicle. If I'm not mistaken, General Mladic's demand was that on the very next day, on the 20th, early in the morning, the evacuation should begin. That evening, I think we got in touch with the political leadership in Sarajevo again, and we conveyed the demands by the Serb side, or, more specifically, General Mladic's demand. At that point in time -- or, rather, at that time, as of the 13th and then onwards, the major problem that we were facing was what to do about the able-bodied men, men of military age, between 18 and 50 to 60 years of age. Our idea was to have all able-bodied men exchanged with the Serb side along the principle "all for all," provided that they were not surrendered or handed over to anyone, because we feared for their lives. I think that the reply we received from Sarajevo was something to the effect that there would be negotiations at the airport and so on to that effect. And the Serb side again interpreted this as our refusal, and the military attacks renewed on the 20th of July, 1995. Let me just note that at this time, in other words, after the 13th, some people began arriving from Srebrenica, people who had tried to cross over, bringing with them the stories of all that they had been through, which further instilled fear in the hearts of the Zepa people, so that the situation at this time was very difficult. Fear was the predominant emotion that the people there had.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you for a moment, sir. One quick question. You mentioned a colonel, and I think it came out as "Pusic." Is that the correct name or was -- is it a different name?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it should read "Kusic," K instead of P. And I said that as far as I could recall, I believe that Colonel Kusic, Rajko Kusic, also attended that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And during this meeting on 19 July, sir, were you aware that it was being video-recorded?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we were aware of that, because as soon as we arrived, there was a reporter or a cameraman - I believe he was with the army of Bosnian Serbs - and he was there throughout the conversations and throughout the meeting there, and we were aware that this was being video-recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You told us a couple of moments ago that the reports that began to arrive in Zepa from people who had survived or had knowledge of what happened following the fall of Srebrenica, to use your words, and I quote, "further instilled fear" in the population of Zepa. Now, presumably shelling would instill fear in anyone, but can you tell the Trial Chamber why the Zepa population was further instilled with fear? What were they afraid of? Please share that with the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when I said that people began coming from Srebrenica, if we think of the dates, these could only have been those people who had tried to cross over to the territory under the control of the BH Army and who did not succeed in that, but they managed to pull out and come back to the Zepa territory, going through some villages in the Srebrenica area and so on. So these were stories and reports by those people who were in the column; not the ones who went from Potocari, but others who tried to cross over and who were unsuccessful, but who managed to come back. So the stories came from those people. As for the shelling, I will now be a bit, well -- I'll use some grim humour or joke. But shelling was a daily occurrence at the time, so that did not cause any fear anymore. And I'd like to repeat that as of the 13th and onwards, the main fear was how all this was going to end. It was clear that Zepa had to fall. We were perfectly clear on that, and we were just looking for ways to save lives. All our activities and efforts were directed toward that goal. We wanted, and we tried as much as we could, to keep the situation under control. What did that mean? Well, that meant that we tried to always be in touch -- in contact with the UNPROFOR, to maintain contact with the Serb side, and so on, because the center of Zepa was where the UNPROFOR headquarters were. The brunt of the attack of the Serb forces came from the south, and people from all the villages on the southern side, south to south of the Zepa River, had already evacuated and moved into the hills, so there was the fear that if everyone were to withdraw and we lost contact with the UNPROFOR, that then the entire population of Zepa would find itself in a very difficult situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, from the period of 13 July up until these reports started coming in about Srebrenica, you just told us that you were already afraid for the fate of the military-aged men of Zepa even before the reports started coming in. Please tell the Trial Chamber why you were so afraid for the fate of the military-aged men of Zepa even before you began getting reports about what happened after the fall of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look. At the time, and it was wartime, the fear for the fate of military -- for the fate of people was widespread because, in Zepa, we knew about a lot of what had happened, especially in view of the reports from Eastern Bosnia, reports by the people who had survived, so it was a general belief that if one were to fall into the hands of Serbs, if they were to be taken prisoner, that they would not survive, that they would be killed. So this was what the fear of the able-bodied men rested on. This fear, of course, grew over the past three or four years, and it was a general view held by all able-bodied men, or most of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, again, even before the reports about what happened following the fall of Srebrenica came in to Zepa, referring now to the elderly, the young, the children, the women of Zepa, based on your experience, and tell us what -- your state of mind and the state of mind of those you knew in Zepa at the time, what kind of life did you -- could you expect for those people had they tried to stay in Zepa following the Serb attack?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please clarify which group of people you're referring to, which group, what part of the population?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Again, I'm referring to the Muslim women, children, elderly, non-able-bodied men, sir. Focusing on that group of the population, the question is: Even before these reports about what happened following the fall of Srebrenica came in, what kind of life did you or could you expect they faced had they remained in Zepa following the VRS take-over of Zepa which you expected would be certain, would be inevitable?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, that option, to remain in Zepa, was not even entertained, probably because of the fear and the general sense of insecurity and the fact that some 90 [as interpreted] per cent of the population in Zepa were refugees, so this was not their home. 60 per cent, I said, not 90 per cent. So that this option, the option to remain there, was not even entertained. There was fear. Zepa had to be evacuated and territory exchanged, and whoever was there at the time could very well understand the fear that prevailed at the time. And I would like to stress one more time that to remain in Zepa at that time, especially after the 20th, was not a realistic option, and no one actually considered it. Everyone was aware of the fact that Zepa had to be evacuated.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So please pick up, sir, where you left off. I believe you had returned to Zepa with Mr. Kulovac. And if you could just finish off with the events of the 19th of July, and then we'll look at some video footage.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe that I said all there was to say about that story, but I will try to go back. So after this meeting at Boksanica, where General Mladic was in attendance as well, where he dictated his demands regarding the evacuation of the civilians and the surrender of able-bodied men or soldiers, we returned to Zepa that afternoon. As far as I can remember, we got in touch with the political leadership in Sarajevo that same afternoon, asking them to try and agree with the Serb side on the exchange of military-aged men from Zepa along the principle "all for all," so that they should be exchanged for all Serb prisoners of war. And I believe that the answer was something to the effect that there was to be a meeting on the next day or the day after. The Republika Srpska Army continued their attack on the next day, the 20th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now -- sorry, Witness. If you had something to add about the events of the 19th, please do. What I'd like to do, if you're -- if you have nothing further to add, is to show some video. I see you shaking your head no. Okay. Before we --

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have nothing to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Before we look at some video, Mr. President, if we could just go into private session for one question that will, I think, enable us to watch the entire video in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, Ms. Stewart will play one portion of the compilation tape that we've listed on our exhibit list, and this is from 65 ter 6417. I believe it picks up at 2 minutes and I think it's 46 seconds of the compilation, just for the record, for the future, so we know where to start. We do have English and B/C/S transcripts which have been up-loaded into e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't see a thing.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "If General Smith or anyone from UNPROFOR comes by, I will tell them that it's me, and they will already be there. A jeep is already waiting for me in Zepa, actually."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, we've paused at 3 minutes and 29 seconds of the video. Do you recognise the individual at the far right of this still here?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's General Mladic on the very right.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recognise the individual in the blue helmet?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's Colonel Dudnjik.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Please continue. And, Mr. President, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just having a technology discussion, Mr. President, with the Court's indulgence. Okay. Can we continue, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Black Sea. I will visit the Black Sea." "Good. Your wife and children ..." "Finish the war here. Come on." "I will visit you." "Could we try the old --" "I didn't understand." "Come on."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, we've paused at 4 minutes and 32.9 seconds. Do you recognise the individual pictured here with the cigarette in his hand?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Dudnjik, Sejmon Dudnjik.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "General Mladic, I'm listening. "General Mladic speaking. General Mladic speaking. Let me talk to Avdo Palic. General Mladic speaking, General Mladic speaking. Let me talk to Avdo Palic." "Dudnjik? Here's Dudnjik." "Avdo, this is General Mladic speaking. Do you read me? Copy? You can rest assured. Take your deputy or any UNPROFOR officer, take any of your associates and one woman, and come here to the UNPROFOR check-point so that we can agree on further rescue of the entire population and safe evacuation. Do you understand me? Over." "Mr. Palic, I decide about the venue and the people I will talk to, not you. I can give you my word, as an officer and a general, that you are completely safe. Come with one of your associates, the one you choose, one woman that you choose, and an UNPROFOR officer of your choice. Whether it's going to be Dudnjik's deputy or not, that's up to you. I had talks and I saved civilian population, and everyone who listened to me from Srebrenica, and I talked to Mr. Nesib Mandzic, UNPROFOR commander, and a certain Mrs. Camilla. I give you my word as an officer that the passage is free. Come here and we will agree on all the details. Do you understand me? Over." "Mr. Palic, I am not interested in Rasim Delic or Alija Izetbegovic or Karadzic. I'm interested in the fate of the people who have been misled, and I don't want the innocent to suffer. I want to resolve this, and I want to give you a chance. There's no need for you or the people to die. You have a chance. Come and take it. You will not get it again. Make no mistake. Do you understand me? Over." "Mr. Palic, I call the shots and I say who's coming. I am General Mladic. You have half an hour, starting now. Call me if you want to negotiate, and this is your last chance. We will not talk again. In that case, you have signed a death sentence for everyone in the territory controlled by you. Do you --"

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, just to set a little bit of the context here, from what location is General Mladic speaking here, just to leave no doubt for the record?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe -- and not only do I believe, but I know that this is check-point 2, manned by UNPROFOR, at Boksanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And where was Mr. -- or Colonel Palic located during this conversation?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Palic, on the other side, was in Zepa, in the elementary school in Zepa which housed the UNPROFOR base for Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how do you know he was there during this conversation?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was with him during that conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And for the record, we've paused at 10 minutes 12.7 seconds. Please continue, Ms. Stewart. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Do you understand? Over." "Mr. Avdo, you report to whoever you want. I have another obligation as a human being and as a general. Let me talk to someone more sensible than yourself, because you are fighting for your life and you are capable of sacrificing the people for your sake and the sake of your own ass. Let me talk to that woman and the other guy who is with you. I cannot talk to you. If you want, come and I will listen to you, so that I can see what you want and if we can resolve the problem. Whether I have the authority or you do, we should leave that for others to judge. I am giving you a chance to settle this as men, because you have shed enough blood here, you and your followers. And I'm telling you you should put this lady on the phone so I can talk to her, as a woman, because women are more sensible than you, who are misguided by ideology. And I did not come here to argue with you. I came here to give you and your people a chance. Do you understand me? Over." "Avdo, I'm trying to understand you. There's no need for people to suffer because of you and your skin. I guarantee you full freedom, and I will go where -- you will go where you want me -- where you want to go, but try and help stop the bloodshed. Did you get that? If you're not capable of that and you can't do it, put one of your associates on, let me talk to somebody else, so that I have clear conscience with regard to what I intend to do if you continue being unreasonable. Over." "I think I sent you one litre of brandy from Rogatica, and I signed a box of cigarettes for you. To tell you the truth, it was a long time ago, but I know that I sent all that. I believe that it was a box of Drava cigarettes or something like that. Believe me, Avdo, I'm giving you a chance, both to you and your people. I want to keep my humanity when all this is over, and, trust me, you have to trust me. You will return to your people, and let us cut this Gordian knot in a nice and human way." "Avdo, did you get that? Over." "Listen, this is Hamdija Torlak, a representative of the Zepa municipality." "Mr. Torlak, greetings to you, and I am inviting you and Mr. Avdo Palic, and bring a woman with you or someone else if you need them. Bring an UNPROFOR officer and come to this check-point at Boksanica. I will receive you with my associates to resolve the issue, so that the people in the territory do not suffer. I guarantee you full freedom both on the way there and on the way back. Do you understand me? Over." "You are controlling -- I don't know. Well --" "Mr. Torlak, if you want, take four APCs, UNPROFOR APCs, or one, just let me know and I will give an order for the passage to be freed, and you will arrive here completely safe. Do you understand? Over." "I understand completely. If you could --" "Do not delay so much. I don't have the time to wait for you for hours. The night's falling. I'm giving you 30 minutes. You have until 1700 hours. That's enough. Discuss it and let me know. And then there is also enough time for me to tell my men whether you are coming and how, to order the road to be cleaned for your safe passage. Do you understand? Over." "I do. So we will talk again at 1700." "Okay, I agree. I will order my men to be ready to let you through from 1700 on. First of all, you will help your people greatly, but me as well, because I don't wish to have anybody on my conscience. I'm here to help you. I'm the only one who can help you at this moment. You can be sure of this. And I can help you only with your help. There is no need to turn this terrain into a venue of tragedy of both mine and your people. Okay, thank you, and bring a woman with you, if possible." "Well, I will check. You know how it is. I --" "Okay, I will talk to you at 1700 hours. I will order my men to ensure the passage from Zepa to Boksanica, to this check-point. You will just tell me the names of the delegation members, you will tell me who the UNPROFOR officers and soldiers are." "Okay." "We will see. If there are barricades, we will remove them." "Okay, I'll talk to you at 1700, General." "Good luck. We'll talk at 1700 hours."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, when, in relation to your -- the meeting you described, when you sat down with Generals Mladic and Tolimir, did the conversation we just heard take place, approximately? We don't need a specific time, if you can't recall. But approximately what time did that conversation occur?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the afternoon, in the second half of the day. The meeting wasn't long. According to my estimate, it was not longer than 30 to 40 minutes. And the conversation took place at check-point 2 in Boksanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Before we go to the next portion of this video, I note, again, we do have both English and B/C/S transcripts available in e-court linked to this exhibit, if that helps the interpreters at all. We also have hard copies of the B/C/S transcript, if that will assist the interpreters. Again, the video is subtitled, but we do have the transcripts available, electronically and hard copy, to hopefully make the job a little easier for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: They should be given to the interpreters to be of assistance for them, or was that already provided?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just available in e-court, Mr. President. But we do have hard copies, if they prefer hard copies, and we can hand that up right now. And for the record, we'll be starting at page 8 of the B/C/S transcript. And we'll continue at 18 minutes 15.5 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "They told you already yesterday, the day before yesterday, to surrender your weapons, surrender your ammunition. You said, We will die. They were waiting the whole night to attack us, and they will wait during the whole night for the Muslims to attack."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "Srna, Srna, Srna, this is Panorama 01. Respond. Over. Give me Srna, personally." "Andric, I'm at Kusic's. I'll wait for you at the check-point. I'm waiting for the Turks to come and negotiate."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, we've paused at 21 minutes 29.8 seconds. Do you recognise anybody in this still, starting from left -- I beg your pardon -- from right to left?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that a question for me?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. On the far right we see General Tolimir. Centrally is General Mladic. And on the far left, I believe this is Kosoric, an officer of the Republika Srpska Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you. We can continue, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "General, it was here where we brought -- and from here, it was a clearing, because like this you cannot -- you cannot with Zolja." "He comes to this curve in the road and cannot -- when we brought in our forces from here --" "We are here now, right now." "How do you say 'boring' in Ukrainian?" "Which gate? That's another gate." "What kind of question is that?" "So the dog won't bite them." "No, he won't. He's quiet." "Here it is. Now, we came to try to arrange one thing."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, we've paused at 26 minutes 25.3 seconds. There is an individual seated with his back to the camera, wearing a military cap. Can you identify who that is for the record, please?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's General Zdravko Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue.
