Again, for anybody that wants to follow along with the B/C/S transcript, it is in e-court, and we have made the Word versions of those transcripts available to the Defence for some time. We can certainly get by just by watching the video with the subtitling, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The English text of the transcript should be available, anyway. Perhaps you can up-load it into e-court as well, if it is not done yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: It is already up-loaded, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "I'm not going to use the term which you --" "Well, they should just inform them that we cannot establish communications with them, only through the UNPROFOR communications." "There are children and some women."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We've paused at 27 minutes 42.1 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you that you are pausing. At the moment, we have to discuss the matter of the audio and the recognition of the voice. Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: This clip, I think, has about eight minutes left, Mr. President, so it's no problem to pause it here. We may even be able to resolve the technical glitch in the meantime, and we'll liaise with the booth about that as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In fact, we have already interrupted this video because of our technical discussion, so that I think it is appreciated that we have now our second break. And we will resume at 6.00, and hopefully it will be possible to resolve the technical problem with the voices to be heard. We adjourn and resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think we've solved the technical problems that we had earlier. We will -- instead of playing this off the Sanction system, we'll play it from a CD. The audibility of Colonel Palic during that conversation is very poor, so I don't think any -- there's much enhancement we can do to get that so that we can hear it, for example. I think you can make it out if you're a B/C/S speaker and you listen to it carefully. So I propose that we start with the events at the UN check-point in Boksanica, when General Tolimir and Colonel Kosoric arrive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Very well. Very well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Let's roll the video, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We don't have interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The video is in Russian. We do not interpret from Russian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Why don't we start with the beginning of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We'll do that, Mr. President. And in light of the proceedings thus far, because we have the subtitles and because everything, I believe, will be sufficiently audible for all the parties, I propose that we can suspend the double-interpretation, as it were, and just listen to the events and follow along for the English speakers on the subtitles, and for the B/C/S speakers it will all be in the native language, anyway, and we can go directly to the meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I was told, for the sake of the record, that everything that was audible or readable was translated into B/C/S for the accused. If that is the case, I think we can proceed in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And for the record, we're at 23:46 of the CD video, and we have a -- there's a seven-second difference between the time of the video that we're showing from the CD and the time that is up-loaded into e-court. So just for the future purposes, if we're going back to look at the record, we just have to take that into account, in terms of locating positions on the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We should have the video in evidence as well. The CD, yes, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We can do that, Mr. President. Okay, let's roll the video, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, we're pausing at 27 minutes 36 seconds. I just wanted to ask the witness a question about this passage right here.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: There's a reference, sir, to wounded, and some of them being women and some children. How were they wounded, sir?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the women and children must have been wounded in the shelling. And as for the men, they might have been wounded either on the front-line or also during the shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Please continue with the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We're pausing at 31 minutes 43 seconds of the video. Just a couple of questions, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Most recently in the video, General Mladic referred to a Merdjan or a Mrdjo. Do you know about whom he is speaking there?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that was a Republika Srpska Army soldier who was wounded or lightly wounded in an operation conducted by the BH Army to the north-west of the enclave, somewhere on the Serb territory. That soldier was in Zepa since that time, the time of that operation. Later on, I learned that he had been taken to the check-point and handed over to Republika Srpska Army. I did not take part in that exchange. I only heard of it later. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately when, during these events, this VRS soldier who had been captured by the ABiH was returned to the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what we saw here was the 19th of July, so I think that that must have been on the 20th or the 21st at the latest. So it would have been on the following two days, in my assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, was anyone actually exchanged for this VRS soldier or was he simply turned over to the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he wasn't exchanged. He was just turned over to the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, finally, there was -- there were a couple of references to a location called Brezova Ravan. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what that location is and what its significance was at the time?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Brezova Ravan is a locality. It is not a settled -- it's not a settlement. It's on the road between Zepa and Boksanica. It's in a dominant position so that it commands the view of Zepa, and it's possible to control Zepa -- the center of Zepa from there. The Brezova Ravan was also the place where the first line of defence of Zepa was. At this time on 19th of July, the BH Army soldiers were still on Brezova Ravan, in that location.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And during July of 1995, sir, if one wanted to drive from the center of Zepa up to Boksanica, would one necessarily have to pass through Brezova Ravan?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know any other road that could take you to Boksanica up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's continue playing the video, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We're pausing at 34 minutes 46 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you identify the man who's in the center of the frame here, please?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's Colonel Sejmon Dudnjik.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's continue with the video, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, we're pausing at 35 minutes 10 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Of the men in uniform, can you identify any of them, moving from left to right on the screen?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: From left to right, the first one is General Mladic. Then comes General Tolimir, then an officer of Republika Srpska Army whom I recall. I recall his face, but I don't know his name. I don't know the next person either. And then I believe this is Colonel Kosoric, if I am not mistaken, but I can't really say that with certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just for the record, the man you believe is Colonel Kosoric, is he clean-shaven?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He has a moustache.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's continue playing the video, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: When we left off before showing the video, you had brought us basically to 20 July. Did the military or civilian authorities from Zepa respond to the demands that you told us General Mladic made at this meeting? And if not, can you describe, please, for the Trial Chamber what happened then, starting with the 20th of July forward?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recall -- I would just like to briefly comment on this video-clip that we've just seen. I believe that a portion was cut out where we hear the conditions that General Mladic dictated, and it relates to what it is -- what was to be done with the able-bodied men. I believe that he said there that they should surrender their weapons, that they should go to the UNPROFOR, be registered for an exchange "all for all." As far as I can recall the meeting of the 19th, it should have been there. That portion is missing. And now I can return to your question as to what happened after this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just to clarify, sir, have you ever seen video footage of what you are telling us you recall General Mladic saying? Have you ever actually seen that on video footage at all?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean in reference to what I've just said, according to my recollection, what was missing on this video footage? Well, I can't really confirm that. I can't say that I've seen the video footage before, although it is possible to obtain it. And I think I did see it a long time ago. But why did I say this? Well, in further developments, we returned to Zepa, me and Benjamin Kulovac, where the evacuation of the civilian population was no longer questionable. We were certain that it would proceed as planned, that there wouldn't be any problems. However, the problem remained of what was going to happen to the men, the able-bodied men, men of military age, between ages of 18 and 55 to 60 years of age. You could all see in this video-clip that General Mladic, or maybe someone else, said that the dead-line was 10.00 on the 20th of July, when the first group or the wounded should be there to be evacuated. When we returned to Zepa, I think that the entire War Presidency went to the Communications Centre on Zepa Mountain on the 19th, in the evening, and this was the only link -- the only communication line open with Sarajevo. And I believe that on that evening, we talked to Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, then the president of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in which we asked that Minister Muratovic, and I believe he was the minister who was to liaise with the UNPROFOR and international organisations, so we asked that he urgently establish contact with the Serb side in order to ensure that an exchange be implemented on the principles of "all for all." In other words, all able-bodied men from Zepa to be exchanged for all prisoners of war taken by the BH Army, Serb prisoners of war. I don't know exactly and I can't recall whether we received a promise -- a firm promise to that effect, but on the next day, on the 20th of June, we did not proceed to evacuate the population because that issue remained unsolved. We tried again. I believe that in the morning already, we continued this communication, but I wasn't there. But I know that people did not come there, they did not gather to be evacuated. And I believe that on that day, the attacks by the Serb Army on Zepa continued, and I believe that they were even fiercer than so far, than earlier. Those attacks -- let me just briefly go back to something. So on the 20th, as far as I can recall, I spent that whole day on Zepa Mountain, and I believe that on that day this soldier - I believe his name was Merdjan - was taken to the UNPROFOR check-point and handed over to the Serb side. I did not participate in that, but I believe that Benjamin Kulovac told me about it. So the attacks resumed. The situation was getting more and more unpredictable for us. And I believe that at this time, the civilian population from the southern parts, the hills on the southern parts, had already moved to Zepa Mountain. And then on the 24th, or maybe the 23rd, the 23rd of July, the key elevation, key for the defence of Zepa from the south, Brezova Ravan, had fallen. I'm sorry, I think this was on the 24th, in the morning, that -- in other words, on the 24th of June, 1995, Brezova Ravan, as the key elevation, the key position for the defence of Zepa, for the defence of the center of Zepa, fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I just wanted to interrupt you quickly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, just a moment. Judge Mindua has a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not a question, but I just wanted to check something out. On page 60, line 16 of the transcript, the 24th of June is mentioned. Line 25, again, the 20th. We don't know if it's June or July. And on page 61, line 9, the 23rd of July is mentioned. Further down, line 11, the 24th of June. So what is this about? What month are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I would have to see the context in order to determine the month, and I don't have any context here.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If I -- if I may, with the Trial Chamber's permission. His Honour Judge Mindua anticipated my intervention, actually. That was the same question I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: There were two references to June of 1995 in your prior answers. One was, I believe, 24 June, and the other one was 20 June. During the course of your testimony for the last 10 minutes, were you ever referring to June of any year or were you referring to July?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: All those things were happening in July, so there has to be "July" everywhere. However, I believe that I used the right name of the month. There must have been a mistake in the interpretation, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No biggie. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 24th of July, the key elevation for the defence of Zepa, the so-called Brezova Ravan elevation, fell, and the Army of Republika Srpska established new lines and approached Zepa to some 500 and -- or 60 metres as the crow flies from the center of Zepa. That was the closest distance that they reached and that's where they stopped. What ensued was another invitation delivered by the same means, which means that we received information from UNPROFOR. And I believe that the invitation was issued by General Mladic, who was at check-point 2, and he again requested to talk to us at another meeting. The situation in Zepa was quite dramatic, bordering on chaotic. People were scared, on the brink of panic. To the best of my recollection, Benjamin Kulovac and I communicated via radio and discussed our options. I believe that Mr. Benjamin did not agree to go, to use that term. I told him, I'm going, because we have a problem on our hands and we have to deal with it. At the UNPROFOR check-point, I went there in an UNPROFOR vehicle, escorted by two foot-soldiers, two privates. I believe that some captain was supposed to be with us, but he had found a good reason not to go. We went there in the afternoon, late afternoon, on the 24th of July. Even before Brezova Ravan, we encountered a VRS check-point. To the best of my recollection, I remember that the car we were travelling in, the UNPROFOR car, had a problem. That's why we had to pull over at Brezova Ravan. And the car remained behind, and that's why we proceeded towards Boksanica, to check-point 2, in a VRS vehicle. And the two UNPROFOR soldiers were also with me in the car. And when we arrived at the same place where the meeting on the 19th of July had taken place, we found General Mladic there, and perhaps even General Tolimir. But I'm speaking from memory, and I can't be sure of that without any corroborative materials. And some other VRS soldiers that I'd seen before. I believe that Dudnjik was there, representing UNPROFOR. I arrived on my own. Mladic was very angry. At the very outset, he handed me a paper to sign. To be honest, I had expected a different forum, a different format of the agreement. However, that was an agreement on the disarmament of the army, and in the text of the agreement one of the points was also the evacuation of the civilian population. I said to General Mladic that I was not authorised to cover the military or deal with any military issue, but the answer was that for the evacuation of the civilian population to start, the agreement had to be signed and that I could then convey all of the messages to Colonel Avdo Palic. And in that situation, I remember that I even spotted a grammatical error that was subsequently corrected in that document. I signed the document, and I returned to Zepa. Let me just point out that us members of the inner War Presidency had agreed before I departed that all of those things had to be accepted and agreed to, because most of the civilian population had already arrived in Zepa Mountain, north of Zepa, which means that the southern part of the enclave had already fallen. And if everybody had withdrawn to Mountain Zepa, then we would have lost contact with both -- with UNPROFOR, and the complete population, primarily the women, children and elderly, would have been put in a very difficult position. As I returned to Zepa, I was awaited there, of course, by Benjamin Kulovac, and I suppose that Avdo Palic was also there, Colonel Palic. Mehmed Hajric, the president of the War Presidency as well. And together, we went to Zepa Mountain again, because we wanted to inform our political and military leaderships about what had been signed. And when I say "our," I mean Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, who represented the political leadership, and General Rasim Delic, who was the commander of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I remember that we stayed on line for some hour or even two hours, and as far as I remember, what was said was, Okay, let the women and children go. And we kept on insisting that we should find a solution for the able-bodied men. However, no concrete or clear signal, response, or promise was given to us, as far as I can remember. On the following morning, which was on the 25th of July, 1995 -- and before I continue this sentence, let me just briefly go back to my last meeting which took place on the 24th July at Boksanica. Amongst other things, what was agreed on that day was some details of the evacuation. That implied that the International Red Cross teams would arrive in Zepa, and some others, perhaps, and that they would be all escorted by UNPROFOR, and so on and so forth. I don't remember whether it was said clearly at that point that the evacuation from Zepa should be led by General Tolimir. And on the following day, I remember, sometime in the morning, not very early, though, a team of the International Red Cross came. General Tolimir came with his escorts. Colonel Palic was also there, I was there, and some other members of the War Presidency. Should I proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, let me just interrupt you right there and dwell a little bit longer on the events prior to 25 July, and follow up a little bit. You described a little while ago that after the meeting on the 19th, when there was effectively no response from the Zepa authorities to the VRS, you described that the attack became fiercer, more intense. Can you describe for the Trial Chamber what you mean by that and what was being targeted?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the line of defence came under the most fierce attack, and the shelling of Zepa also intensified. I remember that I could no longer approach the building where I worked, and that was a building in the center of Zepa. This is what I remember clearly. The defence lines, especially the one facing Brezova Ravan, came under heavy shelling. And I also heard that the attack had been launched from the south-western side and that it was stepped up. Throughout all that time, the center of Zepa was being shelled and targeted. As far as I can remember, I was at the UNPROFOR base there, and I remember that even the UNPROFOR base came under attack, that it became a target of shelling. That's what I meant when I said that the attacks became fiercer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And were there any targets - let's focus on the center of Zepa - that you would characterise as military targets?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the center of Zepa, there are no military targets. We're talking about five or six buildings altogether. There is nothing that, in my view, could be proclaimed a military target. There are two schools, elementary schools - one is old, one's new - a residential building for the teachers, the building that we used as our headquarters, the executive board and the police. I don't think that those can be qualified as militaries targets. There was also a residential building for the police officers, and there was a mosque. So those buildings constituted the center of Zepa at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how about elsewhere within the enclave during this intensified period of shelling from the 19th through the 24th of July? Were there strictly military targets that were being shelled or were there other targets as well?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I spent most of the time in the center of Zepa, and that's what I could observe. But let me just say that we're talking about villages with nothing but residential dwellings. There's no other type of buildings at all. There are no military targets, as such, something that could qualify as a legitimate military target. And I'm talking about all of the villages around Zepa. That applies to all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Tell the Trial Chamber why Mr. Kulovac did not want to attend the meeting on the 24th of July.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that he feared for his personal safety, that he feared that something bad would happen to him. His personal safety was at stake, I believe, and that's why he was afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: When you signed this agreement on the 24th of July, would you describe for the Trial Chamber what choice you had? If you could explain a little bit further why you signed that agreement and the choice that you felt you had in signing that.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, let me tell you something about my own feelings. I was a bit distracted. Let me not even mention that I was afraid. But, actually, I was not even afraid any longer. Fear was not -- no longer part of my emotions. And as far as our choices went, well, we didn't have any. We were forced to sign whatever text they served us. As long as it ensured the beginning of the evacuation, whatever it may have been, I would have signed it. That's how we decided before I left Zepa. There was no alternative.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And a little while ago in your testimony, sir, you referred to the women, children, and elderly who were fleeing to Zepa Mountain, and you said that they would have been in a -- in the words you used, "difficult position." Can you again please elaborate a little bit? Explain, and you can be as undiplomatic with me as you like, sir, what you mean by that, please.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, this is what I mean: Somebody who left their home could carry only a limited quantity of food or anything else, clothes or I don't know what. They left, and they found shelter in some make-shift buildings, as I later heard. Furthermore, all of that could have gone on for days. If somebody was sick, they could not be provided with any medical assistance. And, finally, what next? Zepa Mountain is just a plateau, an elevation, where the entire population of Zepa would have moved, including the military. I'm sure that the VRS had already started encircling the entire plateau, so there will be civilians which could not live for longer than four or five days. The area is very narrow, there's limited space. It would have been a catastrophe, and I'm sure that even more fierce attacks on the part of the VRS would have ensued. So when I said that the situation would have been difficult, I meant that the situation was extremely dramatic. Well, picture this: For example, somebody with a young child goes to a forest. Of course, they cannot organise their life properly. And you have to know that there was shelling going on, no conditions for a normal life in place. That's what I meant when I used the term.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I see we're out of time for the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sir, you have to realise we have to adjourn now, but we will resume tomorrow in the afternoon again, and your examination-in-chief and later on the cross-examination will continue. Let me remind you again that you shall not talk to either party about the content of your testimony. We adjourn and resume tomorrow in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 25th day of August, 2010, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.03 p.m.,
